Hazards_Annotation: The cyclone's intensity is highlighted by its wind measurements, with the Fiji Meteorological Service estimating 10-minute sustained winds of 150 km/h (90 mph) and the JTWC reporting 1-minute sustained winds of 165 km/h (105 mph).

Time_Annotation: Tropical Depression 16F formed on March 17 and strengthened into Tropical Cyclone Wati on March 19 north of New Caledonia. Later, Wati passed between Lord Howe Island and Norfolk Island and became extratropical on March 25.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The cyclone formed north of New Caledonia; a cyclone watch was issued for Lord Howe Island and a cyclone warning for Norfolk Island; additionally, the remains of Wati brought heavy rain and strong winds to the North Island of New Zealand.
Main_Event_Annotation: The system strengthened into Tropical Cyclone Wati on March 19 and further intensified into a Category 3 cyclone on the Australian scale, which classifies the event under Tropical Storm/Cyclone.
Hazards_Annotation: The remains of Wati brought heavy rain and strong winds—with gusts of 140 km/h reported at Cape Reinga—indicating hazards of both wind and potential flooding.

Time_Annotation: Gonu developed from a persistent area of convection in the eastern Arabian Sea on June 1. Later, it weakened and made landfall on the easternmost tip of Oman late on June 5.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The cyclone caused about $4.2 billion in damage and 50 deaths in Oman, and in Iran, the cyclone caused 28 deaths and $215 million in damage.
Main_Event_Annotation: Gonu made landfall on the easternmost tip of Oman, becoming the strongest tropical cyclone to hit the Arabian Peninsula.
Hazards_Annotation: The storm rapidly intensified to peak winds of 240 km/h and dropped heavy rainfall—up to 610 mm—resulting in flooding and heavy damage.

Time_Annotation: Early on June 21, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) declared the area a depression and later upgraded it to a deep depression. The deep depression made landfall near Kakinda early on June 22 local time.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The IMD declared the system 430 km east-southeast of Kakinada, Andhra Pradesh, India, and the article later notes that the storm killed at least 140 people in India, with another 213 deaths in Karachi, Pakistan.
Main_Event_Annotation: The text details that the system was upgraded to a deep depression and that the JTWC issued its first warning on Tropical Cyclone 03B, indicating the event falls under the Tropical Storm/Cyclone category.
Hazards_Annotation: The article mentions winds near 30 knots and reports warnings of heavy rains and wind from the Pakistan Meteorological Department, supporting the identification of wind and flood as hazards.

100 in the North-West Frontier Province.[38]
Over 80 people were killed in floods associated with the remnants in Afghanistan.

Time_Annotation: The JTWC noted in its Significant Tropical Weather Outlook for the North Indian Ocean on June 24, issued a second TCFA early on June 25 as the system crossed into the Arabian Sea, and the storm made its second landfall around 0300 UTC on June 26 with the final advisory issued later that day.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The cyclone made landfall along the Makran coast near Ormara and Pasni in Balochistan province (Pakistan) and affected regions such as Karachi, Balochistan, Sindh, and the North-West Frontier Province; additionally, heavy floods associated with its remnants caused over 80 fatalities in Afghanistan.
Main_Event_Annotation: The PMD referred to the deep depression as Tropical Cyclone Yemyin and the IMD later upgraded the system, retroactively naming it Yemyin, which classifies the event as a Tropical Storm/Cyclone as per the association table.
Hazards_Annotation: Observations recorded winds of about 26 knots off the Pakistan coast and heavy downpours that flooded the Kech Korandi riverine and the city of Turbat, with additional flooding causing significant casualties in both Pakistan and Afghanistan.

Event_Names: Northern Indian Ocean Tropical Cyclone Season
Time_Annotation: The monsoon became active in May as water temperatures became warm. Twin depressions formed during June on opposite sides of India, which helped intensify the monsoon over the country. The IMD began naming tropical cyclones within the basin in 2004, beginning after the monsoon season. As such, only two cyclonic storms in the latter half of the year were named.

Main_Event_Annotation: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) was designated a Regional Specialized Meteorological Center by the World Meteorological Organization to monitor and warn on tropical cyclones in the northern Indian Ocean.
Hazards_Annotation: No explicit hazards such as wind, flood, or lightning were mentioned in the text.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Oman's most damaging storm was Cyclone Gonu in 2007, which was the strongest recorded storm in the Arabian Sea and the strongest to make landfall on the landmass.[11][12] Gonu left US$4 billion in damage and killed 50 people, making it the worst natural disaster on record in Oman.[13]
In 2010, a slightly weaker cyclone named Phet caused US$780 million in damage and 24 deaths while crossing eastern Oman.[14][15]
Cyclonic Storm Keila in the subsequent year killed 19 people while looping near Oman's southern coastline,[16][17] and left US$80 million in damage.[18]
In 1890, a storm killed 757 people when it flooded much of Oman's capital.[19]
A storm in 1959 caused a shipwreck near southern Oman, resulting in the loss of all 141 crewmembers.[19][20]
Another storm-related shipwreck killed 18 people in December 1998.[21]
In June 1977, a storm struck Masirah Island, causing 105 deaths and becoming Oman's worst natural disaster in the 20th century.[22][23]
A storm in 2002 that killed nine and caused US$25 million in damage.[24][25]
Cyclone Nilofar in 2014 killed four people from its outer rainbands.[26]

Although storms rarely strike Yemen,[6] back-to-back cyclones Chapala and Megh hit the country one week apart in November 2015.[27] Chapala earlier struck the Yemeni offshore island of Socotra, which was also hit by Cyclone Megh less than a week later.[27] The two storms collectively killed 26 people in Yemen.[29]
The country's worst natural disaster on record was from a 1996 storm that earlier hit Oman,[30] causing severe flooding that caused US$1.2 billion in damage and 338 deaths.[31][32]
The second worst natural disaster in Yemen was from a weak depression in 2008 that killed 180 people and caused US$874.8 million in damage.[6][11][33]
More recently, Cyclone Sagar killed a woman when her house caught fire due to the storm.[34]

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Num: 77 homes; town hall, two schools, and an airfield
Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: On Maupiti, an island with a population of 1,100, about 95% of the infrastructure was destroyed. The town hall, two schools, and an airfield were destroyed.[1] In addition, 77 homes on the island were destroyed. All but three homes that belonged to Mormons on the island were destroyed.[14]
On Bora-Bora, an island which had a population of 4,500 at the time, roughly 30% of the infrastructure was destroyed, including 309 houses.[1]

On the north side of Bora Bora, nearly everything was destroyed, including the village of Vaitape and a local yacht club.[16] Across Vaitape, roads were blocked by fallen trees and telecommunication lines were severed due to high winds.
In another archipelago, 700 homes and various public infrastructures were at least somewhat destroyed by Osea.[18]
Several roofs were blown off of buildings across the archipelago.[11]
Hotels were also impacted during the storm.[15]
A Latter-Day Saint meeting house was used as an emergency shelter, though the house itself sustained minor damage from the storm.[13]

Time_Annotation: The season officially began on May 15 in the Eastern Pacific, and on June 1 in the Central Pacific; both ended officially on November 30.

Main_Event_Annotation: The article notes that overall 20 tropical cyclones formed, with 17 reaching tropical storm intensity, 10 becoming hurricanes and eight becoming major hurricanes – a clear indication of a tropical storm/cyclone season (highlighted by events such as Hurricane Otis).
Hazards_Annotation: Hurricane Otis underwent explosive intensification from a tropical storm to a Category 5 hurricane, indicating powerful wind hazards, while Hurricane Hilary’s heavy rainfall led to widespread flooding and mudslides.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: In November 1970, the Bhola cyclone struck what is now Bangladesh and killed at least 300,000 people.
The deadliest was Cyclone Nargis, with at least 138,374 deaths when it struck Myanmar.
In recent years, the deadliest Atlantic hurricane was Hurricane Mitch of 1998, with at least 11,374 deaths attributed to it.
The deadliest Atlantic hurricane overall was the Great Hurricane of 1780, which resulted in at least 22,000 fatalities.
The most recent tropical cyclone with at least 1,000 fatalities was Storm Daniel in 2023, which killed at least 5,951 people.

Time_Annotation: Once over open water, the depression intensified into a cyclonic storm on the morning of June 9. The cyclone quickly weakened to a deep depression overland and tracked west over central India, where it degenerated into a broad area of low pressure on June 11.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The cyclone made a second landfall near Balasore in northern Orissa, affected high rainfall in Orissa and West Bengal, and brought severe rain to Vidarbha and southern Madhya Pradesh in central India.
Main_Event_Annotation: The text states that the depression intensified into a cyclonic storm, indicating a Tropical Storm/Cyclone event.

Time_Annotation: A low-pressure area that had developed over the northern Bay of Bengal on June 28 organized into a depression early on June 29. It degenerated into a remnant low over central Uttar Pradesh during the evening of July 3.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The depression brought intense monsoon conditions to Orissa, Madhya Pradesh and Vidarbha during its life, and later its weakening phase over northeast Madhya Pradesh and central Uttar Pradesh indicates these areas were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: The system intensified as it moved northwest, becoming a deep depression shortly before it crossed the Orissa coast, indicating a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: Recorded winds of 85 km/h and heavy rains (over 210 mm in some areas) led to overflowing rivers in Orissa, flooding of rice paddies in Cuttack District, and the Wainganga River overflowing its banks.

Time_Annotation: The system intensified as it moved to the northwest, becoming a deep depression on July 7, and its remnant low persisted until July 12 when it was absorbed by the monsoon trough.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The depression made landfall on the Orissa coast, brought isolated heavy rains throughout East India, and its remnant low moved north over western Bihar.
Main_Event_Annotation: The system evolved from a depression into a deep depression – a classification that falls under the tropical cyclone category.
Hazards_Annotation: Winds of 55 km/h were recorded at peak intensity and the depression brought isolated heavy rains (over 100 mm per day), indicating the hazards of wind and potential flooding.
